title: 3994. Minimum Adjacent Swaps to Partition Array

examples.explanation: Swap nums[1] and nums[2]. The array becomes [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. This array is good because it can be split into [1, 2], [3, 4], and [5, 6].

One sequence of optimal swaps is as follows: Swap nums[2] and nums[3]. The array becomes [9, 7, 3, 5]. Swap nums[1] and nums[2]. The array becomes [9, 3, 7, 5]. Swap nums[0] and nums[1]. The array becomes [3, 9, 7, 5]. Swap nums[1] and nums[2]. The array becomes [3, 7, 9, 5]. Swap nums[2] and nums[3]. The array becomes [3, 7, 5, 9]. This array is good because it can be split into [3], [7, 5], and [9].
The array is already good. No swaps are needed.

hints: Replace each element with its group number: 0 if it is less than a, 1 if it is in the range [a, b], and 2 if it is greater than b.
After this replacement, the goal is to make the array sorted in non-decreasing order.
With adjacent swaps, the minimum number of swaps needed is the number of inversions in this group array.
Since there are only three possible group values, scan from left to right and count how many previous values are greater than the current value.
